The claim's method acknowledges the definitional mismatch but then models it as two-sided: the ci80 upper bound of $0.033 implies 322bn queries for 2007, i.e. 26.8bn/month - below comScore's own measured 37.1bn for August. The upper bound is not reachable on the claim's own denominator source.

new.method: Numerator: Google web-sites advertising revenue 2007 = $10,624.705m (Form 10-K FY2008, grade A). Denominator: comScore qSearch measured 37.1bn Google searches worldwide in August 2007, but on a Age-15+, home-and-work basis that excludes public terminals, mobile phones and PDAs - so it is a floor, not a point estimate. Growth-adjusting August back to a calendar-2007 average gives ~34-35bn/month (~410-415bn/yr) on comScore's basis, which sets the interval's UPPER bound for revenue per query ($0.028 at 380bn). The central assumes a modest allowance for comScore's exclusions (~483bn queries, 40bn/month) giving $0.022; the lower bound assumes a 1.5x correction (~664bn queries) giving $0.016. The old interval treated the denominator error as two-sided and its upper bound implied 26.8bn queries/month, below comScore's own August measurement.

verdicts.reason: Interval challenge: the denominator's known error is one-directional (comScore systematically undercounts) but was modelled symmetrically, and the upper bound sat outside what the cited source can support. Central shifts down accordingly.

verdicts.evidence: Both paths reproduce exactly. Upper path: FY2008 10-K gives 2007 cost of revenues $6,649.085m and total TAC $4,933.9m; the difference is $1,715.2m, and 1,715.2/415bn = $0.004133. Lower path: 319/111,000 = $0.002874, matching Kelly's $0.0028. The central of $0.0035 sits between them and the ci80 [0.0020, 0.0055] brackets both. The shared 415bn denominator inherits the comScore undercount flagged at e6-unit_econ-001 - a higher query count would pull the upper path down to roughly $0.00355 - but that lands well inside the stated interval, so the claim absorbs the correction without a change. Grade C correct.

verdicts.disagreement: If e6-unit_econ-001's denominator is revised upward as recommended, this claim's central would drift toward $0.0032. It stays inside the interval either way, so I am not forcing a change - but the two claims should be recomputed together, not separately.

verdicts.evidence: Two independent defects. First, the stated method does not reproduce its own interval: 'combining the endpoints of the two component intervals (revenue $0.018-$0.033, cost $0.0020-$0.0055)' gives (0.018-0.0055)/0.018 = 69.4% and (0.033-0.002)/0.033 = 93.9%, i.e. [69, 94], not [76, 92]. Second, and more useful, the query denominator CANCELS out of a margin - so this claim should never have inherited the query-count uncertainty at all. Computed directly from the filings, margin = 1 - 1,715.2/10,624.705 = 83.9%, with no query estimate anywhere in it. The real uncertainty is cost allocation: a Kelly-style narrow non-TAC operating cost (~$1,276m/yr) gives 88.0%, while loading a full share of 2007 R&D ($2,120m) drops it to 63.9%. The sanity checks in the method are all correct (2007 gross margin 59.93%, operating margin 30.64%, TAC 30.1% of advertising revenue).

old.method: CI derived by combining the endpoints of the two component intervals (revenue $0.018-$0.033, cost $0.0020-$0.0055).

new.method: The query denominator cancels, so compute the margin directly from the FY2008 10-K rather than from the two per-query components: 1 - (non-TAC cost of revenues $1,715.2m / Google-web-sites advertising revenue $10,624.705m) = 83.9%. That is a floor on the owned-search margin, because the $1,715.2m also carries network ad serving, content acquisition, credit-card fees and amortisation that owned-site queries do not cause; stripping those out moves the figure toward the ~88% implied by a Kelly-style narrow non-TAC operating cost. Central set at 85%. Interval spans 78% (generous cost attribution to owned search) to 91% (marginal serving cost only). It deliberately excludes the 64% figure produced by loading a full share of R&D, which is a company-level, not a per-query, cost. Sanity check: Google's reported 2007 gross margin was (16,594.0-6,649.1)/16,594.0 = 59.9% and operating margin 30.6%; the per-owned-query margin is higher because it excludes TAC (30.1% of advertising revenue in 2007), a distribution cost rather than a serving cost.

verdicts.reason: The stated CI-construction method was arithmetically wrong for its own inputs, and the whole construction was unnecessary: the margin is query-independent and can be read straight off the filings, which both tightens the interval and removes its dependence on the contested comScore denominator.
verdicts.disagreement: Researcher propagated per-query uncertainty into the margin. That double-counts an error that appears identically in numerator and denominator; the margin is the one unit-economics figure in this era that does NOT need a query estimate.
